Tanzania bolsters economic ties with China at BRI forum in transport, energy, communications
NAIROBI: TANZANIA has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening economic cooperation with China through the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), focusing on strategic projects in transport, energy, communications and infrastructure to boost economic growth, expand trade and investment opportunities, and improve citizens’ livelihoods.
Speaking on behalf of the Minister for Finance at the Belt and Road Initiative Forum in Nairobi, Kenya, Deputy Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Finance Asha Khamis Abdulla said cooperation between Tanzania and China had continued to create development opportunities in infrastructure, trade, investment and industrial transformation.
Asha said Tanzania regarded the BRI as an important platform for strengthening economic and financial cooperation among countries while promoting sustainable and inclusive development aligned with national development priorities.
“The longstanding relationship between Tanzania and China, built on mutual respect, trust and solidarity, has continued to strengthen cooperation in infrastructure, trade, investment, energy and industrial transformation,” Asha said.
ALSO READ: Tanzania, China agree to bolster TVET system to equip youth with industrial skills
She emphasised that Tanzania would continue working with China and other countries to implement development projects aligned with national priorities and the goals of Development Vision 2050, with the aim of improving productivity, stimulating economic growth and enhancing citizens’ welfare.
In a related development, Asha said Tanzania, in partnership with Zambia and China, was pursuing plans to revive and upgrade the Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority (TAZARA) through a public-private partnership (PPP) arrangement.
She said completion of the project was expected to improve transport efficiency, reduce freight costs and facilitate regional trade, thereby stimulating economic activity and strengthening market connectivity across Southern Africa.

articles.title: Trade Intelligence Tools to Boost Nigeria’s Exports, Investment - Voice of Nigeria
articles.summary: Trade Intelligence Tools to Boost Nigeria’s Exports, Investment  Voice of Nigeria
articles.full_text:
Nigeria is stepping up efforts to convert rising capital inflows and export growth into industrial expansion and job creation through new trade intelligence tools designed to help businesses access international markets, navigate trade requirements and strengthen export competitiveness.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Jumoke Oduwole, said the tools would provide Nigerian exporters and investors with reliable market information to guide commercial decisions and translate economic reforms into measurable gains for the real economy.
Speaking at the launch of the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment’s Trade Intelligence Tools in Abuja, Oduwole said the initiative aligned with President Bola Tinubu’s ambition to build a one-trillion-dollar economy by 2030.
READ ALSO: Nigerian Navy to Establish Defence Technology Research Institute
She cited an increase in capital importation from about 3.9 billion dollars in 2023 to more than 23 billion dollars in 2025, while non-oil exports reached approximately 12 trillion naira, with Nigerian products reaching more than 120 countries.
The minister also disclosed that intra-African trade grew by 21 per cent in 2025, stressing that the priority was to translate these gains into productive investment, completed export transactions and stronger domestic industries.
“Our task now is to turn capital flows into productive investment, export opportunities into completed transactions and policy reforms into measurable gains in the real economy,” Oduwole said.
She acknowledged persistent challenges confronting businesses, including high production costs, limited access to finance, logistics constraints and complex trade procedures. According to her, the government is working with private-sector and institutional partners to address these barriers.
Oduwole explained that the tools would help exporters identify promising markets, understand applicable tariffs and entry requirements, and access reliable information before shipping their products.
They would also provide investors with clearer information on Nigeria’s productive capacity and investment opportunities.
She identified the forthcoming CANEX Weekend 2026 and the Intra-African Trade Fair 2027 in Lagos as strategic platforms for expanding commercial partnerships, promoting Nigerian products and connecting businesses with international buyers and investors.
The minister said the ministry planned to formally launch its Trade Portal at CANEX Weekend, scheduled for November 5 to 8, 2026. The portal is expected to connect businesses with market intelligence and help turn trade contacts into actual transactions.
Presenting an overview of the ministry’s trade intelligence publications, the Minister’s Special Adviser, Dr Tochukwu Nwachukwu, highlighted developments in exports, investment inflows and Nigeria’s expanding trade relations.
Nwachukwu disclosed that the ministry’s latest Trade Intelligence Report showed that Nigeria’s non-oil exports reached a record ₦12.36 trillion in 2025, while capital importation nearly doubled over the period.
He said the reports were developed to strengthen evidence-based policymaking, improve accountability and provide reliable data for government, businesses and investors making trade and investment decisions.
According to him, the ministry produced two publications: the Trade Intelligence Report 2026, which analyses trade and investment performance throughout 2025, and Trade in Six Months: Nigeria Half-Year 2026, which covers developments between January and June 2026.
Meanwhile, the President of the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA), Jani Ibrahim, called for increased private-sector investment in value-added exports, competitive manufacturing and priority export value chains to strengthen Nigeria’s position in global trade and generate more jobs.

articles.title: Nigeria’s non-oil exports hit record N12.36tr, expands to 120 countries - The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.summary: Nigeria’s non-oil exports hit record N12.36tr, expands to 120 countries  The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.full_text:
Nigeria’s non-oil exports reached N12.36 trillion in 2025, with shipments to more than 120 countries, as the Federal Government stepped up efforts to diversify exports and strengthen domestic production.
The Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment disclosed this in a media update yesterday, adding that non-oil products accounted for 14.5 per cent of total exports in 2025, up from 11.7 per cent in 2024.
The number of distinct non-oil products exported also rose to 281 from 246, while Nigeria’s intra-African trade increased by 21 per cent. The number of certificates of origin issued under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) grew by 500 per cent during the period.
Despite the gains in exports, manufacturing and trade made a smaller combined contribution to Nigeria’s economic growth in 2025 than in the previous year.
According to the ministry, the two sectors contributed 0.43 percentage points to real gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 3.87 per cent in 2025, down from 0.46 percentage points in 2024, when the economy grew by 3.38 per cent.
Trade contributed 0.31 percentage points, compared with 0.35 percentage points in 2024, while manufacturing’s contribution increased to 0.12 percentage points from 0.10 percentage points. Manufacturing grew by 1.41 per cent in 2025, up from 1.2 per cent in 2024, while trade growth slowed to 1.77 per cent from 1.97 per cent.
The ministry said foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows improved to $920 million in 2025 from $680 million in 2024. Total capital importation rose to $23.22 billion from $12.32 billion, although the ministry acknowledged that direct investment remained modest.
It also reported stronger manufacturing performance in the first quarter of 2026, when the sector grew by 3.29 per cent. Cement production expanded by 11.53 per cent, pharmaceuticals by 6.15 per cent, automotive assembly by 5.44 per cent, and food, beverage and tobacco by 4.10 per cent.
Vehicle assembly increased by 40.6 per cent in 2025, while cassava starch production rose by 474.74 per cent and light electronics production by 16.67 per cent.
To deepen domestic value addition, the ministry is developing a framework to guide the allocation of shea nuts to local processors before any surplus is exported. The current ban on raw shea nut exports expires on February 25, 2027.
Trading on the Nigeria Commodity Exchange also expanded, with volumes rising to 24,668 tonnes in 2025 from 3,942 tonnes, while traded value increased to N4 billion from N1.9 billion.
The ministry said special economic zones had created more than 20,000 direct jobs. It is also targeting the completion of the export component of the National Single Window by November 2026 to simplify trade procedures and improve export processing.
It added that it was pursuing coordinated tariff reviews to balance government revenue needs with the protection and growth of domestic industries.

articles.title: The Accra Reset: Africa’s United Call To End Raw Mineral Exports And Build Industrial Prosperity - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: The Accra Reset: Africa’s United Call To End Raw Mineral Exports And Build Industrial Prosperity  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
Africa stands at a defining moment in its economic history. For generations, the continent has supplied the world with valuable minerals while receiving only a fraction of the wealth generated from their transformation into finished industrial products. Gold, bauxite, manganese, lithium, cobalt and other strategic resources have powered industries across the globe, yet many African economies remain heavily dependent on exporting these commodities in their raw or minimally processed forms.
This longstanding economic contradiction dominated discussions at the second African Minerals Policy Forum–Mining in Motion Summit, reportedly held in Accra from October 19 to 21, 2026, under the theme “One Continent, One Voice on Minerals.”
The gathering brought renewed attention to Africa's determination to move beyond raw mineral exports towards domestic processing, industrial manufacturing, technological development and greater control over its natural resources.
Organised by the Ashanti Green Initiative, with reported support from the African Union and the Government of Ghana, the summit sought to promote a coordinated continental approach to mineral governance, investment and industrialisation.
At the centre of the discussions was a fundamental question: Why should Africa continue exporting the minerals that power global industries while importing expensive finished products manufactured from those same resources?
For Ghana, this question carries particular significance. The country possesses substantial deposits of gold, manganese and bauxite, alongside emerging lithium resources. Yet the economic benefits derived from these minerals have historically been constrained by limited domestic processing capacity and insufficient integration with local manufacturing.
According to accounts of the summit, President John Dramani Mahama reaffirmed Ghana's ambition to move away from exporting unprocessed mineral ores, with 2030 presented as a target for strengthening domestic mineral processing.
Such a policy, if formally adopted and effectively implemented, could represent an important shift in Ghana's industrial development strategy.
Rather than relying primarily on royalties, taxes and export earnings from raw minerals, the country would seek to capture additional value through refining, manufacturing, technology transfer and skilled employment.
Bauxite could support alumina refining and aluminium production. Manganese could provide inputs for steelmaking and battery-related industries. Lithium could create opportunities for mineral processing and participation in emerging energy technology supply chains.
However, the transformation of mineral resources into competitive industrial products requires far more than political declarations.
It demands substantial investment in electricity, transport infrastructure, processing facilities, technical education, research and development, and reliable industrial financing.
Mineral processing is often energy-intensive and technologically demanding. Without affordable electricity, modern equipment and competitive production systems, domestic processing requirements could increase costs and discourage investment.
Ghana must therefore ensure that any restrictions on raw mineral exports are introduced through a carefully sequenced industrial strategy supported by commercially viable processing capacity.
The wider African challenge is equally significant.
Countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia, Guinea, South Africa and Ghana possess important mineral resources, yet much of the higher-value industrial activity associated with these commodities takes place outside the continent.
Africa's participation in global mineral supply chains must increasingly extend beyond extraction to include refining, component manufacturing, engineering services and technological innovation.
This ambition is consistent with the African Mining Vision, adopted by the African Union in 2009, which promotes transparent, equitable and development-oriented exploitation of mineral resources.
The African Continental Free Trade Area also provides an opportunity to develop regional mineral value chains, allowing countries to combine resources, infrastructure, skills and markets rather than attempting to establish every industry independently.
For example, regional cooperation could support mineral processing facilities, shared industrial infrastructure and manufacturing clusters serving multiple African economies.
Such cooperation would strengthen Africa's bargaining position in international markets while creating opportunities for indigenous businesses.
The summit also highlighted the importance of responsible mining and environmental protection.
In Ghana, illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey, continues to threaten rivers, forests, agricultural lands and public health.
The destruction associated with unregulated mining demonstrates that mineral wealth can become a national liability when extraction is pursued without effective governance.
Environmental rehabilitation, transparent licensing, stronger enforcement and improved monitoring technologies must therefore become central components of mineral policy.
Formalising responsible small-scale mining, supporting legitimate operators with technical expertise and enforcing reclamation obligations could help reduce environmental damage while protecting livelihoods.
Equally important is the need to prevent arrangements in which local ownership requirements are circumvented through nominal Ghanaian partners acting on behalf of foreign operators.
Local participation must be genuine, extending beyond ownership on paper to meaningful involvement in financing, management, engineering, procurement and manufacturing.
Traditional authorities, local communities and civil society also have important roles in ensuring that mining contributes to sustainable development rather than environmental degradation and social conflict.
The reported involvement of prominent continental leaders and international institutions at the Accra summit reflects growing recognition that Africa's mineral resources must serve broader development objectives.
Nevertheless, declarations of continental unity must translate into enforceable policies, measurable investment commitments and functioning industries.
Africa has held numerous conferences on resource beneficiation and economic transformation. What has often been missing is sustained implementation.
The continent cannot achieve industrial independence simply by demanding higher prices for raw minerals. It must develop the technical and commercial capabilities required to manufacture competitive products.
This means investing in engineers, metallurgists, geologists, industrial chemists, technicians and entrepreneurs capable of building and managing modern processing industries.
It also requires transparent contracts, predictable regulations and partnerships that promote technology transfer rather than perpetuating dependence.
The growing global demand for minerals used in renewable energy systems, electric vehicles, electronics and advanced manufacturing presents Africa with an important opportunity.
But that opportunity will be diminished if the continent merely replaces its historical dependence on exporting gold, cocoa and crude oil with a new dependence on exporting unprocessed lithium, cobalt and other critical minerals.
The minerals may change, but the underlying economic imbalance will remain.
Ghana and its African partners must therefore pursue a coordinated strategy that combines responsible extraction, competitive processing, local manufacturing and access to regional and international markets.
The success of the Accra discussions should ultimately be measured not by the prominence of participants or the strength of political declarations, but by the processing plants established, technologies acquired, skilled jobs created and additional value retained within African economies.
Africa's mineral wealth must become the foundation of African industrial prosperity, not merely a source of raw materials for factories elsewhere.
The Accra Reset represents an important call for a change in economic direction. Its promise will depend on whether African governments can translate that vision into practical, accountable and commercially sustainable industrial policies.
For Ghana, the challenge is clear: mineral resources must contribute to building industries, developing technical capabilities and expanding economic opportunities for future generations.
Africa must no longer be satisfied with owning the minerals beneath its soil while other nations capture most of the wealth created above it. The continent must increasingly process what it mines, manufacture what it can and retain a greater share of the value generated from its natural resources.
That is the true pathway from mineral dependence to industrial sovereignty.

articles.title: Overdependence on gold, cocoa leaves Ghana exposed to changes in global commodity prices - ISSER - MyJoyOnline
articles.summary: Overdependence on gold, cocoa leaves Ghana exposed to changes in global commodity prices - ISSER  MyJoyOnline
articles.full_text:
Audio By Carbonatix
The Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER) has stated that the dependence on gold and cocoa leaves Ghana exposed to changes in global commodity prices and production conditions.
The country’s external position strengthened considerably in 2025, with export earnings growing much faster than imports.
The merchandise trade surplus widened from US$3.8 billion to US$13.8 billion, while the current account surplus rose from US$1.6 billion to US$9.4 billion. International reserves also increased, strengthening the country’s foreign exchange position, while the cedi appreciated against major international currencies.
However, ISSER expressed worry in its 2025 State of the Ghanaian Economy Report that the improvement was heavily concentrated in primary commodities, particularly gold and cocoa. Minerals accounted for 68.2% of merchandise exports, highlighting continued export concentration.
It explained that although non-traditional exports grew by 30.7%, Ghana’s export base remained relatively undiversified.
“A strong trade surplus does not necessarily indicate that the economy has become more diversified or internationally competitive”, it warned.
Policy Priorities
ISSER called for diversification of exports through expand manufactured and processed exports to reduce commodity dependence.
Similarly, it wants increased domestic value addition that is the strengthening of processing capacity and linkages between agriculture, mining and domestic industry.
Finally, it urged the country to build external resilience via sustain reserve buffers and the strengthening of export competitiveness while reducing vulnerability to commodity price fluctuations.

articles.title: School’s apology flags antizionist stand - South African Jewish Report
articles.summary: School’s apology flags antizionist stand  South African Jewish Report
articles.full_text:
Emmarentia Primary School’s apology for displaying the Israeli flag at a children’s concert has sparked outrage, exposing what critics describe as a troubling double standard at a Johannesburg public school repeatedly used for anti-Israel activities.
The school issued an apology on 14 October describing the display as an “oversight” that didn’t reflect the school’s values or beliefs.
In a letter signed by principal Nadia Variawa, the school apologised for the “hurt and concern” caused and reaffirmed its support for the Palestinian cause.
“Emmarentia Primary School has always stood against the genocide and in support of the Palestinian cause,” the letter stated. “As a secular South African school, our country’s stance remains clear: we stand against apartheid and genocide.”
The school confirmed it had “rectified our error”.
The apology – subsequently removed from the school’s social media platform – has ignited fierce debate about political neutrality in public education.
Danny Mofsowitz, chairperson of the South African Jewish Board of Deputies (SAJBD) Gauteng Council, described both the decision to apologise and its contents as “deeply problematic”.
“A government school should have no qualms about displaying any national flag and shouldn’t single out the flag of the only Jewish State,” she said.
“A statement from a school, which should be apolitical and secular, shouldn’t include deeply divisive and contested terms such as ‘apartheid’ and ‘genocide’ in this context.”
Mofsowitz said the SAJBD had repeatedly cautioned against importing the Middle East conflict into South African communities and schools.
“We have dealt with similar issues at various schools in recent years. We are looking into the best way to address this matter at Emmarentia Primary School, a school that many in our community attended and loved.”
However, a former Jewish teacher at the school has alleged that political activism extended beyond events held on the premises and into the school environment itself.
The teacher, who requested anonymity, told the SA Jewish Report, “During my time at [Emmarentia Primary], I experienced many situations that I found deeply uncomfortable and, at times, antisemitic. These included repeated jokes about Jewish people made by the head of department in my phase.
“When discussions about the Arab-Israeli conflict arose, some members of staff openly expressed their political positions through clothing and symbols, including keffiyehs and abayas bearing messages such as ‘Free Palestine’.”
She said political discussions had also taken place in front of pupils.
“On occasions, I felt I was being viewed through the lens of my religion and the political conflict, rather than simply as their colleague and teacher.
“My concern is the apparent disconnect between the school’s public commitment to humanity, compassion, dignity, justice, and respect for all, and the experiences I had as a Jewish teacher within its walls,” she said.
The South African Zionist Federation (SAZF) said the flag apology was particularly disturbing given the school’s “troubling history of providing a platform for highly politicised anti-Israel activities”. It highlighted events organised by Social Intifada, whose social media profile declares, “By Any Means Necessary.”
On 8 and 9 August this year, the third annual Palestine Youth and Family Market, organised by Social Intifada, took place on the school premises. It featured Palestine-themed children’s activities, political discussions, documentary screenings, and exhibitions.
According to the SAZF, the exhibition included simulated Israeli checkpoints, displays depicting Palestinian prisoners, and bodies wrapped in burial shrouds.
“These aren’t simply cultural celebrations. They are deeply political presentations of a complex conflict, taking place in an environment intended for primary school children,” the SAZF said.
Photos taken by passersby in recent months and seen by the SA Jewish Report show anti-Israel posters on the school’s perimeter fence bearing slogans including “Zionism is racism” and “Resistance against occupation can never be condemned”.
Earlier photos show cardboard cut-outs depicting deceased Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah on the premises, as well as Hezbollah flags.
A mass iftaar, the communal meal breaking the Ramadan fast, accompanied by Palestine-related exhibitions, took place on the school premises organised by the Palestine Solidarity Alliance.
Former international relations minister Dr Naledi Pandor addressed the gathering, making allegations against South Africans allegedly serving in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).
“Who are these 174? Can we get their names? Can we make their names public? Can we let South Africans know what they have done in our name, essentially, by being present in the IDF as the IDF massacres women, the aged, and children?” she said.
Pandor also questioned why these alleged soldiers hadn’t been prosecuted.
During one of these similar events, one display featured a makeshift graveyard of white sticks bearing the names of Palestinians described as martyrs killed in Gaza.
The SAZF said, “That the mere display of Israel’s national flag should warrant an official apology, while such overtly political activities have repeatedly been accommodated on school grounds, speaks to a deeply concerning double standard.
“Schools should be places where children learn, develop independent thinking, and feel safe, regardless of their background or beliefs. They shouldn’t become platforms for political activism or ideological agendas.”
The controversy raises questions about the distinction between allowing outside organisations to use school facilities and a public school’s institutional endorsement of political positions.
Emmarentia Primary is a fee-paying public school governed by the South African Schools Act and falling under the Gauteng Department of Education. Public schools may make facilities available for community activities, subject to applicable legislation and policies.
The controversy carries historical significance in Emmarentia, once home to a substantial Jewish community. The neighbourhood has gradually evolved into a more religiously and culturally diverse area, including a growing Muslim community.
A longtime Jewish resident, who requested anonymity for security reasons, said the controversy reflected what she regarded as a longstanding pattern.
“I’ve lived in Emmarentia for more than 20 years. In the past 15 years, the school has become notorious for taking an active anti-Israel stance, and this embarrassing incident is more of the same,” she said. “Why apologise for displaying the flag of a sovereign nation in the world of nations?”
She questioned whether families holding different views on Israel felt comfortable expressing themselves.
“It’s disappointing that the assumption is being made that the delegitimisation of Israel is mainstream, and everyone approves of it. How is any of this educational or inclusive?”
Johannesburg resident Dianne Kendall expressed similar dismay.
“As a past pupil, I am absolutely disgusted by what has happened,” she wrote on social media. “Children should be allowed to be children. They should be learning about compassion, kindness, critical thinking, and respect for people who may have different beliefs, backgrounds, or identities.
“This is not the Emmarentia Primary I remember.”
In a strongly worded public statement, Pastor Tumelo Thom asked, “Are our schools educational institutions or political campaign headquarters?”
Questions were sent to both principal Variawa and the Gauteng Department of Education, with no responses received at the time of going to print.

articles.title: GoldBod pushes local ownership of mining assets - Business & Financial Times
articles.summary: GoldBod pushes local ownership of mining assets  Business & Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi said Ghana’s mineral wealth must translate into greater domestic participation in mine ownership, financing, engineering, processing and refining, rather than leaving local businesses and professionals concentrated in lower-value activities.
Speaking at the African Minerals Policy Forum – Mining in Motion 2026, he said mineral sovereignty will remain incomplete if financing, technology and the most profitable segments of the mining value chain continue to be controlled externally.
“Mineral sovereignty will remain incomplete if Africans continue to be confined to low-value activities while finance, technology, processing and the most lucrative opportunities remain under external control,” he said.
He argued that Ghana needs deliberate policies that enable indigenous enterprises and young professionals to become mine owners, geologists, engineers, equipment suppliers, financiers, processors, refiners and traders.
The call comes as GoldBod expands its role in formalising the gold trade and strengthening Ghana’s capacity to capture economic value from its mineral resources. Between January 1 and October 20, 2026, the board aggregated and exported 85.4 tonnes of artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) gold valued at US$11.6billion, surpassing large-scale gold exports of 76 tonnes worth US$11.1billion over the same period.
Mr. Gyamfi attributed the performance to reforms designed to bring gold previously lost through smuggling and informal trading into official channels. These include a four-tier licencing regime, competitive pricing, digital stock-booking systems, official receipting and stronger regulatory enforcement.
He said the reforms have helped increase recorded ASM gold exports from 63 tonnes in 2024 to approximately 104 tonnes in 2025, generating US$10.8billion in foreign exchange. This development, he argued, demonstrates how changes to the trading system can improve the formal economy’s capture of mineral revenues without necessarily requiring a corresponding increase in production.
Beyond export earnings, GoldBod is seeking to expand Ghanaian participation across the wider gold value chain. Its institutional, licencing and value-addition reforms have created 4,866 direct jobs in less than two years, comprising 361 public-sector positions and 4,505 private-sector jobs according to Mr. Gyamfi.
He said greater participation in processing, refining, equipment supply and related services can create additional employment and business opportunities, particularly for young people and indigenous enterprises.
As part of efforts to improve the sector’s productive capacity, GoldBod plans to introduce an Artisanal and Small-Scale Mining Formalisation and Financing Support Programme in 2027. The initiative will be implemented with the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources and University of Mines and Technology, with technical support from South Africa’s Rand Refinery.
The programme is expected to improve access to financing and technology, increase gold recovery rates, reduce operating costs and minimise environmental degradation associated with artisanal and small-scale mining.
GoldBod is also working with the Ghana Geological Survey Authority on geological investigations at Funsi in Upper West Region and Bensere, Ashanti Region. The studies are intended to reduce investment risks, develop an investment-grade portfolio of mineral assets and strengthen Ghana’s negotiating position in prospective mining ventures.
Such work can help address one of the constraints facing local participation in mining: the financial and technical risks involved in identifying, developing and operating commercially viable deposits. However, expanding Ghanaian equity ownership also requires access to long-term capital, technical expertise and effective project governance.
The board’s broader strategy includes strengthening national ownership of mineral-related value chains and ensuring that more of the economic returns from mining remain within the country. In 2026, GoldBod also purchased and delivered 1.8 tonnes of large-scale gold valued at US$224million to the central bank in support of accumulating national gold reserves.
Mr. Gyamfi said the objective is to move beyond measuring mineral wealth by extraction and export volumes toward assessing the jobs, industries and economic opportunities generated for citizens.

articles.title: Terry Gale | Mr President, take urgent action to safeguard AGOA benefits - News24
articles.summary: Terry Gale | Mr President, take urgent action to safeguard AGOA benefits  News24
articles.full_text:
Terry Gale, CEO of Exporters Western Cape, calls for urgent action to protect South Africa’s access to the US market in an open letter to President Cyril Ramaphosa. Exporters already face multiple rising pressures and cannot absorb removal from AGOA, he writes.
- For more financial news, visit News24 Business.
Dear President Ramaphosa,
As my recent correspondence with the Presidency indicated, I wish to reiterate the importance of South Africa’s continued eligibility for the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which has been extended until 31 December 2028.
The uncertainty surrounding our trade relationship with Washington comes at a time when exporters are already under considerable pressure from tariffs, declining export values and increasing competition in international markets.
It is totally unacceptable that South Africans should have to “prepare” for the possibility of being removed from Washington’s duty-free trade programme for Africa, given the current impasse between the two countries.
The US president reviews countries’ eligibility for AGOA annually, with any removal requiring 60 days’ notice to Congress and the country concerned.
To take effect on 1 January 2027, an exclusion must be announced by 2 November 2026.
Time is not on our side – hence this plea, as we cannot afford to lose any more jobs, given our untenable unemployment rate.
We need urgent, constructive diplomatic engagement.
It is easy to say that we should replace the US with other export markets; however, it is not that easy, as we have noticed when trading with our BRICS partners.
Try exporting into China, India or Brazil.
Key trading partner
Since AGOA was signed by then-President Bill Clinton on 18 May 2000, the US has become one of the Western Cape’s most important and profitable trading partners over the past 26 years.
The latest 12-month rolling comparison shows that exports fell by 41%, from R16.89 billion between August 2024 and July 2025 to R10.02 billion between August 2025 and July 2026. Exports to the US supported approximately R12.98 billion in provincial GDP, 11 914 direct jobs and 35 467 indirect jobs.
The most affected product categories include fruit juices, with export values declining by 86% (from R953 million to R137 million); grapes by 79% (from R444 million to R91 million); yachts by 55% (from R1.4 billion to R628 million); wine by 38% (from R603 million to R371 million); and citrus by 17% (from R2.19 billion to R1.82 billion).
These figures demonstrate the serious consequences of losing access to the US market. The loss of AGOA eligibility would further undermine South African exporters and place additional strain on an economy that can ill afford further losses.
President Ramaphosa, we recognise that international trade negotiations are complex and that the relationship between South Africa and the US involves issues beyond commerce. Nevertheless, we urge your government to make protecting South Africa’s trade relationship with Washington an economic priority and to pursue every available avenue to resolve the current impasse.
We cannot afford to lose a valuable trading relationship that supports our economy. With South Africa’s AGOA eligibility at risk, urgent action is needed to protect our access to the US market and prevent further damage to exporters and employment.
Terry Gale is CEO of Exporters Western Cape.

articles.title: Egypt, Côte d’Ivoire explore new industrial investments amid banking, trade barriers - Economy - Business - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Egypt, Côte d’Ivoire explore new industrial investments amid banking, trade barriers - Economy - Business  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Egypt is exploring industrial investment opportunities in Côte d’Ivoire in tyre manufacturing, palm oil production, and agro-industries, as the West African country seeks to attract Egyptian manufacturers while banking and maritime trade obstacles remain unresolved.
Egypt’s Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem and Côte d’Ivoire’s Ambassador to Egypt Albert G. Douley agreed to identify industrial projects that could be launched in the near term, aiming to turn bilateral cooperation agreements into investments that benefit both countries, according to a Ministry of Industry statement on Thursday.
However, the discussions also highlighted barriers to expanding business ties, including the absence of an Egyptian bank in Côte d’Ivoire and the lack of a maritime trade agreement between the two countries.
Hashem said the ministry and the Ivorian embassy would examine sectors prioritized in their respective industrial strategies to identify feasible projects based on each country’s capabilities and market needs.
He stressed that implementing concrete industrial projects would be key to accelerating cooperation and overcoming financial and logistical challenges.
Egypt’s Industrial Strategy 2030 identifies industrial integration with African countries as one of its main pillars, providing a framework for expanding industrial partnerships across the continent, Hashem said.
For his part, Douley said Côte d’Ivoire was seeking to attract Egyptian industrial investment, particularly in manufacturing, under its economic development plan through 2030.
The plan identifies priority industrial sectors for private-sector projects, including tyre manufacturing, palm oil production, and agro-industries, which could offer direct investment opportunities for Egyptian companies, he said.
Douley also called for activating cooperation agreements signed during President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi’s visit to Côte d’Ivoire in 2019, citing the convergence of views between the two countries’ political leaderships.
The proposed industrial cooperation would seek to expand commercial and investment links between Egypt and Côte d’Ivoire, with the two sides now set to identify projects that could move forward in the near term.
Egypt’s Africa integration strategy centres on using the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and COMESA to expand exports, build regional value chains, and position Egyptian firms, especially manufacturers and SMEs, across African markets.
The strategy also seeks to address a significant gap: Africa accounts for only about 15 percent of Egypt’s exports, despite the continent’s proximity and market potential.
Egypt views African economic integration as both a foreign policy priority and an export-led growth strategy. Its recent focus has shifted from signing agreements to implementing them by resolving disputes over AfCFTA rules of origin, training exporters, supporting SMEs, strengthening COMESA ties, and directing investment toward neighbouring African markets.

articles.title: Africa CDC calls crisis meeting as Ebola spreads to Nigeria - DW.com
articles.summary: Africa CDC calls crisis meeting as Ebola spreads to Nigeria  DW.comEbola has spread from Congo to 4 other countries. A look at where things stand  CNNNigeria Ebola case matches DR Congo strain  EWNAfrica CDC urges countries to strengthen Ebola preparedness  SABC NewsEbola outbreak spreads to four African countries as WHO sounds alarm  IOL
articles.full_text:
Africa's Center for Disease Control (CDC) late Wednesday announced that it would convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.
What's the latest regarding the Ebola outbreak?
More than 9,500 people have been infected since the virus was first confirmed in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in May. Nearly half of those infected have died.
The Africa CDC announcement followed news on Tuesday that the virus had spread to Nigeria, arriving with a woman who had returned from Uganda earlier in the month.
Africa CDC's Wissam Mankoula said it is still not confirmed that Nigeria's Ebola patient had traveled to DRC. Nigeria and Uganda are sharing information to research the possible source of exposure.
Authorities in Nigeria say they are tracing 44 contact persons, with Health Minister Muhammad Pate noting that officials are, "doing everything possible to contain this case."
Uganda, which recorded 20 cases in this latest outbreak and declared itself "Ebola-free" in July, has rejected Nigeria's claims. The World Health Organization (WHO) declared the Uganda outbreak over on August 27.
Virulent Ebola strain with no approved vaccines or treatments
This current outbreak involves the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which no approved vaccines or treatments exist. The strain was also matched to the patient in Nigeria.
"We did three levels of tests, but all molecular. The strain was Bundibugyo," said Olajumoke Babatunde, director of the public health laboratory service at the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention.
Africa CDC Director General Dr. Jean Kaseya billed the October 28 crisis meeting as a chance to "strengthen our collective response."
In all, the outbreak, which the WHO says is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever, has spread to four countries in Africa and is active in two of them.
One French national, a doctor doing humanitarian work in transmission zones inside DRC was infected but recovered after treatment at a specialized facility in France.
Ebola now impacting three African regions
It has also spread wider than previous outbreaks, reaching central, eastern and western regions across Africa.
Africa CDC's Kaseya made note of this in a post to X late Wednesday, writing: "Ebola is now affecting three regions of Africa. The situation demands urgent action and political leadership at the highest level."
"We must now accelerate our actions, reinforce coordination and mobilize the full strength of our continent," Kaseya's post continued. "Africa has the expertise, the institutions and the capacity to defeat this outbreak. We must act together and we must act now."
For its part, the WHO advised "all countries in the region to sustain a high level of readiness as the DRC outbreak continues to evolve."

articles.title: Kenyan investors eye Africa growth agenda as FT summit convenes global leaders in London - Capital FM Africa
articles.summary: Kenyan investors eye Africa growth agenda as FT summit convenes global leaders in London  Capital FM Africa
articles.full_text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Oct 22– African governments and investors are meeting in London to examine how the continent can mobilise domestic capital, expand regional trade and attract investment as shifting global trade patterns reshape economic opportunities.
The 13th Financial Times Africa Summit, held on October 21–22 under the theme Mobilising Growth in a New Global Order, brings together political leaders, policymakers and business executives to discuss financing, infrastructure, energy and industrial development across African economies.
The discussions are relevant to Kenya as it seeks to attract private investment, deepen regional trade and expand domestic financing for infrastructure and productive sectors amid competition for global capital.
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama and former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo are among the confirmed participants at the summit, alongside Dangote Group President and Chief Executive Aliko Dangote and several African finance ministers.
The agenda places particular emphasis on mobilising domestic capital, scaling small and medium-sized enterprises and strengthening African financial systems as governments seek to reduce barriers to investment and support sustainable economic growth.
Sessions on the first day examined the future of finance, African fintech, gold reserve management and investment opportunities in small businesses, while discussions on the second day focused on trade, capital allocation and the implications of changing international alliances.
For Kenya, the focus on regional markets and alternative sources of investment comes as businesses navigate trade costs, infrastructure financing needs and competition for funding from international investors.
The summit’s discussions on tariffs and shifting trade relationships also highlight the importance of diversifying export markets and strengthening commercial links with major trading partners, including China, India and Gulf economies.
Other confirmed speakers include Mo Ibrahim, founder of the Mo Ibrahim Foundation; Jakaya Kikwete, former president of Tanzania; Ahmed Shide, Ethiopia’s finance minister; and Kristy McNeill, the United Kingdom’s minister for international development.
The programme also covers the Red Sea corridor and US-Africa policy, examining how geopolitical developments could influence trade routes, investment decisions and the movement of goods across the continent.
A separate feature of the gathering is the Africa Sustainable Futures Awards, organised in partnership with the World Bank Group’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA).
The awards recognise private-sector initiatives developing scalable solutions to Africa’s development challenges.
The summit comes as African economies seek to convert their market potential into investment, jobs and higher-value production, with policymakers under pressure to strengthen local financial markets while attracting international funding.
The event’s organisers say the annual gathering provides a platform for African and international decision-makers to discuss the economic and policy choices shaping the continent’s long-term growth.

articles.title: Nigeria’s carbon Market is Working, Says 9JA Carbon Trade, as Kigali Summit Tells Africa to Deliver - THISDAYLIVE
articles.summary: Nigeria’s carbon Market is Working, Says 9JA Carbon Trade, as Kigali Summit Tells Africa to Deliver  THISDAYLIVE
articles.full_text:
Latest Headlines
Nigeria’s carbon Market is Working, Says 9JA Carbon Trade, as Kigali Summit Tells Africa to Deliver
9JA Carbon Trade, a Qietur Limited company, joined 600 delegates from 52 countries at the Carbon Markets Africa Summit 2026, where governments, buyers and financiers were told to stop drafting rules and start closing deals.
Nigerian carbon project developer 9JA Carbon Trade says the Federal Government’s first authorisations for carbon projects show that the country’s system works. The company spoke after taking part in the Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026 in Kigali, Rwanda, which closed on 15 October with a call for Africa to move from writing rules to delivering projects.
delegation,Timothy Solomon and EkeneOkpara at CMAS, Kigali, Rwanda 2026
‘Kigali changed the question Africa is asked,’ said Timothy Solomon, Co-Technical Manager of 9JA Carbon Trade Ltd, a carbon project development company specialising in land use carbon projects. ‘It is no longer whether the continent can supply carbon credits, but whether it can deliver them with integrity, at fair prices and with benefits host communities can see. Nigeria now has the framework and its first approvals. Our part is to bring forward projects worth approving.’
At a session on country readiness on 14 October, Ibrahim Shelleng, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Finance and Stakeholder Engagement, said Nigeria issued six letters of authorisation in March 2026 and two more by September. A letter of authorisation is the government’s formal approval for carbon credits to be used outside Nigeria. In granting one, Nigeria agrees not to count those tonnes towards its own climate target.
Speaking from the floor, Ekene Okpara, Co-Technical Manager, 9JA Carbon Trade, said Nigeria’s progress on authorisations‘gives us confidence as developers that the process works’. He asked whether Nigeria plans a bilateral carbon agreement with another country, and what advice officials had for developers still awaiting approval from the National Council on Climate Change, the body that approves carbon projects.
On 15 October, the company joined a round table at the summit’s solution lab on reducing risk for private investors, which examined political risk, insurance, financing and access to buyers.
Six points of agreement
The summit drew some 600 delegates from 52 countries, representing more than 150 organisations, among them more than 50 investors and buyers. Closing the event on behalf of the Minister of Environment, the Acting Permanent Secretary of Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment set out six points of agreement. These included that integrity creates value, that trust is the currency of the market, and that communities are partners whose benefits must be shared and shown. Africa, the statement said, must capture more of the value it creates rather than simply supply the credits.
Governments were asked to finish their rules, apply them, and publish every authorisation and every transfer. Buyers and investors were urged to ‘move from signals to signatures’ by signing purchase agreements that run for several years at fair prices. Development partners and financial institutions were asked to fund project preparation, which the statement described as the stage ‘where good projects die today’.
Opening the summit on 14 October, Rwanda’s Minister of Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, said: ‘Writing rules is one thing, and running them is another.’ She noted that improved cookstoves account for around 87 per cent of Rwanda’s issued carbon credits, while agriculture has produced ‘barely one per cent’ of voluntary market credits in two decades.
Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, Rwanda’s Minister of Environment delivering her speech at CMAS 2026
Buyers are setting the terms
The International Air Transport Association told delegates that CORSIA, the United Nations scheme for international aviation, becomes mandatory for airlines in 2027, and that credits used under it must carry a government letter of authorisation. Lukas Visek of the European Commission said that under a Commission proposal, the European Union would buy credits covering up to 260 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent between 2036 and 2040.
Quality is now driving prices. Lorna Ritchie of the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market said credits carrying its Core Carbon Principles label sell for about 25 per cent more on average than unlabelled credits. Ratings agency BeZeroCarbon said reforestation credits range from $5 to more than $40, depending on their rating.
The African Union Development Agency (AUDA‑NEPAD) told delegates that Africa still relies on verifiers based outside the continent for more than 90 per cent of verification work, causing up to half of all project delays. Its accelerator programme will help build African validation and verification bodies.
The Africa Carbon Investment and Finance Alliance (ACIFA), launched at the summit on 14 October, will build a platform connecting projects with finance and will report back at the next CMAS. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) offered five forms of support, from building investment pipelines to reducing project risk before carbon revenue arrives.
The closing statement urged Africa to arrive at COP31 next month ‘with one voice and with evidence of delivery’. Maxwell Gomera, UNDP Resident Representative in South Africa, asked each delegate to choose one thing to move forward before leaving Kigali. ‘Give it a name and a date,’ he said.

UN hails Nigeria-Morocco gas pipeline project as booster of Africa’s energy security
Energy
 THE United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) has hailed the Nigeria–Morocco gas pipeline project, describing it as a major initiative for expanding energy access across Africa.
The commission said the ambitious infrastructure project, expected to connect 13 African countries, would strengthen regional energy connectivity and support economic development.
ECA Executive Secretary, Claver Gatete, made the remarks during an interactive dialogue with the UN General Assembly’s Second Committee in New York.
The meeting, held under the theme, “Regional cooperation in an age of fragmentation,” examined how trade, transport and connectivity could accelerate sustainable development.
Gatete identified the Nigeria–Morocco gas pipeline as an important example of cross-border energy infrastructure capable of addressing Africa’s persistent electricity shortages.
He said the commission particularly appreciated the initiative, which was expected to extend natural gas supplies across West Africa and beyond.
Gatete described it as “the gas pipeline which cuts 13 countries,” adding that it would eventually provide energy to many other African countries.
The UN official made the remarks while responding to questions from Member States on regional infrastructure, development financing and economic integration.
The Nigeria–Morocco gas pipeline, also known as the African Atlantic Gas Pipeline (AAGP), is a strategic project jointly initiated by Nigeria and Morocco in 2016.
The project is designed to transport Nigerian natural gas through West African countries to Morocco, with the possibility of extending supplies to European markets.
According to ECOWAS, the proposed pipeline network will span approximately 6,800 kilometres, including about 5,100 kilometres of offshore infrastructure.
The regional organisation estimated the project’s cost at approximately 26 billion dollars, describing it as a major investment in regional energy security.
ECOWAS said the infrastructure would help expand electricity generation, stimulate industrialisation, strengthen agricultural production and create employment opportunities across participating countries.
Gatete said Africa’s inadequate electricity supply remained a major obstacle to attracting investment and achieving the continent’s economic transformation objectives.
He disclosed that approximately 600 million Africans still lacked access to electricity, underscoring the urgent need for substantial investments in energy infrastructure.
The ECA chief emphasised the importance of regional power pools, explaining that interconnected electricity systems could create more attractive environments for investors.
He identified energy connectivity, alongside domestic resource mobilisation and improved creditworthiness, as essential requirements for Africa’s sustainable development.
On continental economic integration, Gatete disclosed that 50 African countries had ratified the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) agreement.
He said 44 of the agreement’s 54 signatories had developed national implementation strategies with technical support from ECA.
According to him, intra-African trade currently accounts for approximately 17 per cent of the continent’s trade, considerably below comparable levels in Asia and Europe.
Gatete said the commission was supporting the development of regional value chains to enable African countries to process their resources, expand manufacturing and trade more competitively.
He maintained that strengthening energy infrastructure, regional trade and connectivity would help Africa translate its abundant natural resources into industrial development and sustainable economic growth. (NAN)

articles.summary: Africa seeks closer BRI cooperation in trade, financing  China Daily
articles.full_text:
China and African countries are seeking closer cooperation in infrastructure, trade and financing to strengthen regional connectivity, expand local industries and support economic growth, representatives said at the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 on Wednesday.
Speaking in Nairobi, Chinese Ambassador to Kenya Guo Haiyan stressed China's commitment to align Belt and Road cooperation with Africa's development priorities.
Guo pledged deeper financial cooperation that would help ease investment constraints and advance projects that benefit communities across the continent.
"We will closely align Belt and Road cooperation with the AU's Agenda 2063," she said, referring to the African Union's long-term development blueprint.
Guo said China would support African countries in pursuing modernization suited to their national circumstances, while expanding trade cooperation and helping local producers capture more value from their products.
The forum, held simultaneously in Beijing and Nairobi, was organized by the Export-Import Bank of China.
Chen Huaiyu, chairman of the Export-Import Bank of China, said the bank would deepen cooperation in railways, ports and energy, while expanding partnerships with financial institutions to support development in countries engaged with BRI.
Over more than a decade, the bank had extended more than 7 trillion yuan ($1.05 trillion) in cumulative Belt and Road loans, with operations covering more than 130 participating countries, he said at the forum in Beijing.
Chen said that future support would target clean energy, the digital economy, agriculture and industrial cooperation, helping partner countries build local industries and strengthen their capacity for independent development.
He said more diverse financing arrangements would help partner countries improve their financing structures while balancing development needs with debt sustainability.
In Kenya, plans to extend the Mombasa-Nairobi standard gauge railway, or SGR, to Kisumu, in western Kenya, illustrate how better transport connections could expand the benefits of infrastructure investment.
Philip Mainga, Kenya Railways Corporation managing director, said that construction of the extension had begun, with completion expected in two years.
"We expect the first phase of the project, extending to Kisumu, to be completed within two years," he said.
Reaching Kisumu would connect the railway to Lake Victoria, opening opportunities to serve regional markets and strengthen the movement of goods through the Port of Mombasa on the coast of the Indian Ocean.
Mainga identified Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Sudan and Rwanda among the countries expected to benefit from stronger regional transport links.
"The extension would help attract more regional cargo through Mombasa and provide an additional route for exports moving from inland production centers to overseas markets, including China", he said.
He said avocados, coffee and tea were among the products that could benefit from greater use of rail freight, noting that much of this cargo currently travels by road.
Kenya's Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi told the Nairobi forum that investment in transport, energy, water and information and communication technology was central to the country's development agenda.
He described the Belt and Road Initiative as an important framework for improving connectivity, expanding trade and widening access to development finance.
Lesotho's Finance Minister Retselisitsoe Adelaide Matlanyane stressed the need for affordable, predictable financing aligned with national development plans and delivering measurable benefits to communities. She said efforts to attract international capital should go hand in hand with expanding access to financial services at home.
"Open finance is not just about cross-border flows, it is about opening systems to our own citizens," she said in Beijing, citing mobile money's contribution to financial inclusion in Lesotho.

articles.title: China zero-tariff scheme creates export and job opportunities, says Tau - thenational.co.za
articles.summary: China zero-tariff scheme creates export and job opportunities, says Tau  thenational.co.za
articles.full_text:
Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau says bilateral trade with China and its zero-tariff preference scheme could give South African exporters greater certainty beyond 2028.
Tau was speaking at a briefing in Pretoria on Thursday on China’s zero-tariff treatment for African countries
He said diversifying South Africa’s export markets would help protect local jobs and encourage investment.
“Diversifying South Africa’s markets is how the government plans to protect South African jobs in an uncertain world. Predictable market access gives investors the confidence to build production in South Africa,” Tau said.
He said the objective was not only to increase trade, but also to support more factories, processing and jobs in South Africa.
“Today’s gathering is aimed at raising awareness of the tariff measure and providing a structured platform to address questions from South African businesses,” he said.
How the scheme works
China’s temporary zero-tariff preference scheme took effect on 1 May 2026 and applies to qualifying South African exports, subject to rules of origin and other requirements.
Tau said the scheme provides duty-free access for South African products, although some tariff lines are subject to tariff-rate quotas.
“South African products that meet the rules of origin can enter the Chinese market without customs duties,” he said.
Tau said that exporters must obtain a valid certificate of origin to qualify for the preference. The South African Revenue Service (Sars) had issued 25 975 certificates of origin between 1 June and 31 August, while customs declarations had increased by 199%.
“Our export-promotion programme with China is moving beyond individual events. We intend to use strategic trade fairs, targeted outward-selling missions, hosted-buyer missions and direct business-to-business engagements to advance clearly identified commercial opportunities,” he said.
Negotiations beyond 2028
Tau said South Africa was in the final stages of negotiating a China-Africa Economic Partnership for Shared Development.
The agreement is expected to provide a framework for South Africa and China to negotiate memorandums of understanding and agreements covering trade, investment, infrastructure and logistics, small businesses and industrial development.
The minister said the framework would also support negotiations on a Southern African Customs Union-China early-harvest arrangement.
The reciprocal arrangement is intended to provide longer-term certainty for SACU countries once the current temporary scheme ends.
Trade expo planned for November
Tau said that from 19 to 21 November 2026, the dtic, the Gauteng provincial government and China’s Hunan provincial government will co-host the China-Africa Economic and Trade Expo South Africa Session at the Sandton Convention Centre.
The event will include an “Export to China” session featuring South African fruit, wine, agricultural products, minerals and jewellery.
Tau encouraged exporters to participate.
He said this followed Deputy President Paul Mashatile’s visit to China to attend the China International Supply Chain Expo in June. China also led a business delegation to South Africa in September for the South Africa-China Trade and Investment Promotion Conference and the ninth South Africa-China Trade Fair.
Expert says benefits depend on implementation
Dr Simphiwe Madikizela, a senior lecturer at Unisa’s Graduate School of Business Leadership, said the arrangement could help South Africa expand exports, attract investment, strengthen industrial production and support employment.
“The importance of the arrangement goes beyond simply reducing tariffs. It is about giving South African businesses greater access to one of the world’s largest consumer markets and creating a more predictable environment in which exporters can plan for the future,” Madikizela said.
He said the arrangement could improve the competitiveness of qualifying South African products by reducing customs duties in China.
Potential beneficiaries could include agriculture, fruit production, mining, minerals and value-added manufacturing, she said.
“If exporters can increase sales and secure long-term contracts, the benefits could extend beyond large companies to small businesses, suppliers, logistics operators and workers throughout the value chain,” Madikizela said.
He added that certainty beyond 2028 would be important for businesses considering capital investment, equipment purchases, market development and new jobs.
However, Madikizela said safeguards would be needed to protect South African industries and employment.
“Trade liberalisation must expand South Africa’s productive capacity rather than undermine the industries that support domestic employment,” He said.
The arrangement should therefore be implemented in a way that allows exporters to benefit from improved market access while supporting local manufacturing and protecting legitimate industrial interests from unfair competition, added Madikizela.
